clue.text: One's boy touring northern Majorca, perhaps

parts.note: one is I, and the apostrophe s is added

indicators.note: to tour a place is to travel all round it, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: a lad is a boy
N is the standard abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: Someone's son is on holiday, travelling around the north of Majorca.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' gives I plus the apostrophe S. 'Majorca' seems to be the place toured, but with 'perhaps' it is the definition, an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Majorca is one example of an island in the Mediterranean, and the word perhaps signals a definition by example.

clue.text: Spanish gentleman from south in French orgy — not half!

indicators.note: not half means only half is kept, so the back half of the word is thrown away

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for south
en is the French word for in
taken as written, before it is cut in half

explanation.surface: A Spanish gentleman from the south at a French orgy — and the setter's shocked 'not half!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' reads as a British exclamation meaning 'very much so', but it tells you to keep only half of ORGY.
explanation.definitionFit: Señor is the Spanish title and form of address for a man, equivalent to Mister or sir.

clue.text: A companion met initially in eg NAAFI

parts.note: taken as written
a crony is a close friend or companion

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: the first letter of met

explanation.surface: Two friends first met in the NAAFI, the canteen for British servicemen.
explanation.walkthrough: The NAAFI (Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes) runs canteens and shops for the British forces; the surface makes it a place, but it is an example of a word built from initials.
explanation.definitionFit: NAAFI is pronounced as a word and formed from the first letters of Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes, making it a classic example.

clue.text: Follow divine being going towards heaven?

indicators.note: in a down clue, heading skywards means reading from the bottom up, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: a god is a divine being

explanation.surface: An invitation to follow a deity as it ascends to heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: The heavenly surface suits a divine being, but 'going towards heaven' only works because this is a down entry, which is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To dog someone is to follow or trail them closely and persistently, like a hound tracking its quarry.

clue.text: Naval hero in the hold!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the admiral who won at Trafalgar in 1805
second meaning: a wrestling grip applied from behind the opponent

explanation.surface: A naval hero is down in the hold of his ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'hold' looks like the cargo space of a ship, which fits the naval hero, but here it is a wrestling hold. Horatio Nelson is Britain's most famous admiral.
explanation.definitionFit: Admiral Horatio Nelson is Britain's great sea commander, and a nelson (full or half) is a wrestling grip locking the opponent's arms.

clue.text: Strangely, he'll start to need visa for city in America

indicators.note: done strangely means done in an odd way, so the letters come out in an unusual order

parts.note: the contraction with its apostrophe dropped

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is used

parts.note: the first letter of need
taken as written

explanation.surface: Oddly, a traveller will first need a visa to enter an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a travel oddity, but 'for' is only a link word and 'Strangely' tells you to rearrange HELL, N and VISA.
explanation.definitionFit: Nashville is the capital of Tennessee in the United States, famous as the home of country music.

clue.text: Short story put up in the language of Juvenal

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up means writing it bottom to top, so it runs backwards
something cut short loses its end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a tale is a story
taken as written

explanation.surface: A short story is published in the language a Roman poet wrote in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' looks like publishing or displaying the story, but in this down clue it turns the shortened story upwards. Juvenal was a Roman satirical poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Juvenal wrote his Satires in ancient Rome, so the tongue he composed them in was the classical language of Rome.

clue.text: Eccentric no longer on patrol?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: read as two words, a police officer who has left the round they walk

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the answer into two words: a constable's beat is the area they patrol, so one who has finished is off it.
explanation.definitionFit: The single word means unconventional or quirky, while the split phrase describes an officer who has left their patrol route.

clue.text: Angriest after dispersing one of several elements

indicators.note: to disperse is to scatter in all directions, so the letters are scattered and regathered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The angriest member of a crowd, once the crowd has broken up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angriest' is a whole word that happens to contain exactly the right letters; 'after dispersing' means once those letters are scattered.
explanation.definitionFit: Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon form a group of unreactive noble gases, so this is one member of that chemical family.

clue.text: Note very loud quarrel

parts.note: ti is a note of the sol-fa scale, also spelt te
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A musical score's instruction, or a noisy argument between two people.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical surface suits both halves: a sol-fa note and a dynamic marking.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiff is a minor, short-lived squabble or petty disagreement, especially between friends or lovers.

clue.text: Club I run round November

parts.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
a round shape is the letter O
November is N in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone describes their club's jogging route around the month of November.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like a container signal wrapping one piece around another; here it simply supplies the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf, an iron is a type of club with a metal head, used for shots of middling distance.

clue.text: Commercial vehicle to give way briefly — then moved forward

indicators.note: said briefly means cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: an ad is a commercial on television
a van is a vehicle
to cede is to yield or give way

explanation.surface: A delivery van yields to traffic for a moment and then pulls forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial vehicle' reads as one phrase for a van, but it splits into a TV advert and the van itself.
explanation.definitionFit: To advance is to go forward, so the past tense means moved or went forward.

clue.text: A bishop posted: "Look up: they aren't there!"

parts.note: taken as written
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
posted a letter means sent it

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the word is turned backwards

parts.note: to see is to look

explanation.surface: A bishop puts up a notice telling people to look for those who are missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look up' reads as a single phrasal verb, but 'up' works alone, reversing the word for look in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Absentees are people who are missing from a place where they were expected to be present.

clue.text: Dye ignited letters from Greek

parts.note: lit is the past tense of light, to ignite
mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet, and its plural is mus

explanation.surface: A dye set alight, or characters taken from a Greek text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters from Greek' suggests picking letters out of a word; it means more than one Greek letter mu.
explanation.definitionFit: Litmus is a dye made from lichens, used as a chemical indicator that turns red in acid and blue in alkali.

clue.text: Dip provided by slimmers, excellent

indicators.note: what is provided by a phrase is supplied from within it, so the letters are there in the run of text

parts.note: runs from the third letter of the first word to the first letter of the second

explanation.surface: Slimmers have come up with an excellent low-calorie dip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dip' looks like a party snack for slimmers, but it is the verb, and the answer runs across the comma between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To dip something is to plunge or submerge it briefly in a liquid, which is to immerse it.

clue.text: Messenger dined on stage

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing on another comes after it, so the first piece follows the second

parts.note: a leg is a stage of a journey or race
to dine is to eat, so dined gives the past tense

explanation.surface: A messenger has a meal on a theatre stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage' suggests the theatre, but it is a stage of a race or journey.
explanation.definitionFit: A legate is an envoy or ambassador, especially one sent by the Pope to carry messages and represent him.

clue.text: Decline to prepare to put ball in pocket?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an idiom for deteriorate or fall into ruin

definitions.text: prepare to put ball in pocket
definitions.meaning: second meaning: read literally, a snooker player moving to sink a ball

explanation.walkthrough: 'Decline to' reads as refusing to do something, but 'to' only joins the two meanings. In snooker and pool, to pot is to hit a ball into a pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means deteriorate or be ruined, and taken literally it describes a player about to sink a ball.

clue.text: Prominent position of deep hole in fence, not the first

indicators.note: one thing placed inside another sits within it
not the first means leaving off the opening, so the word's first letter goes

parts.note: taken as written, before its first letter is dropped
a mine is a deep hole dug in the ground

explanation.surface: Describing where a deep hole in a fence stands out most.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deep hole in fence' reads as damage to the fence, but the hole goes inside what is left once the fence loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An eminence is a piece of rising ground, or figuratively a position of fame and distinction above others.

clue.text: Poke after mounting for example dark horse

indicators.note: in a down entry, mounting means climbing upwards, so the letters read from the bottom

parts.note: eg is the abbreviation for for example
a dun is a horse of dull greyish-brown colour

explanation.surface: Poking a dark horse after climbing into the saddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mounting' pictures getting on a horse, but in this down clue it turns the whole string upwards. 'Dark horse' is not the idiom for an unknown contender.
explanation.definitionFit: To nudge someone is to prod or push them gently, usually with the elbow, which is a poke.

clue.text: As I see it, a large book

definitions.meaning: first meaning: read as two words, a phrase meaning in my opinion
second meaning: a big, heavy volume

explanation.surface: Someone gives their opinion that a book is a big one.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening phrase is an everyday opinion marker; split the answer into TO ME and it means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A tome is a book, especially a heavy, weighty or scholarly volume of great size.

clue.text: Monsieur is, I hesitate to say, a penny-pincher!

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for the French title Monsieur
taken as written
er is the sound made when hesitating

explanation.surface: A speaker reluctantly admits that a Frenchman is stingy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I hesitate to say' reads as polite reluctance, but it supplies the filler sound of hesitation.
explanation.definitionFit: A miser hoards money and hates spending it, so someone who pinches every penny is exactly that.

clue.text: Walked in time with stick

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
a rod is a stick

explanation.surface: Someone marched in step, keeping time with a walking stick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walked in time' reads as marching in step; the definition is the single word before 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Trod is the past tense of tread, which means to walk or step on something.

clue.text: Daydreamer spies cat wandering

indicators.note: something wandering strays from its path, so the letters roam into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A daydreamer notices a stray cat roaming about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spies' looks like the verb of the sentence, but its letters join those of 'cat' to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapist retreats from reality into fantasy, which is what a daydreamer does.

clue.text: Lettuce is firm against spades

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
S is the card abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: A gardener's lettuce stands firm against being dug up with spades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' seems to describe the lettuce's crispness, but it is a noun meaning a business.
explanation.definitionFit: Cos is a variety of lettuce with long, crisp upright leaves, known in America as romaine.

clue.text: Screen almost camouflaged small secluded spot

indicators.note: camouflage disguises the look of something, so the letters are disguised by rearranging
almost means not quite all, so the word stops one letter short

parts.note: taken as written, before its last letter is dropped
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A hideaway spot is nearly hidden behind a disguised screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screen' and 'camouflaged' both suggest hiding, which fits the definition, but SCREE plus S is simply rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A recess is an alcove or hidden nook set back from the main space, a sheltered secluded place.

clue.text: Anger after day's work sending things up?

indicators.note: one thing coming after another is placed behind it, so the first piece follows the second

parts.note: Sat is the abbreviation for Saturday, and the apostrophe s reads as is
ire is anger

explanation.surface: Someone is furious after a long day at the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Day's work' reads as a phrase about labour, but the definition starts at 'work', and 'day' is just a weekday abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Satire is a literary or dramatic piece that mocks its targets, and sending up is British slang for mocking.
